description:
ASTRA is a proposed astronaut-health monitoring platform designed for long-duration space missions.  This model integrates biological data, behavioural shifts and radiation exposure records to identify unusual health trends and provide explainable insights, helping astronauts make informed medical decisions where immediate healthcare is not available.

Team members should be passionate about clinical effects of space missions and willing to work together to effectively put together a model !
summary: ASTRA  is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support platform designed for astronauts on long-duration missions, including lunar exploration and journeys to Mars. As crews travel farther from Earth, communication delays and technical difficulties can make immediate medical guidance difficult to access. ASTRA addresses this challenge by bringing health and spacecraft environmental monitoring together in one interactive dashboard. Astronauts can record and track health indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, sleep, cognitive performance and physical health, alongside environmental readings including cabin pressure, carbon dioxide, oxygen partial pressure, temperature and humidity. An interactive 2D body map lets users select organs and body systems to view measurements, graphs and trends. ASTRA compares readings with reference ranges and individual baselines, highlights unusual changes through colour-coded alerts, and provides step-by-step guidance on verifying readings and deciding when to contact crew medical support or Mission Control. Cognitive exercises and health records further support monitoring of wellbeing and performance. Designed to work offline, ASTRA keeps information and guidance accessible when communication with Earth is limited. It does not replace medical professionals; it helps astronauts understand their health, respond to concerns and make informed decisions when immediate support is unavailable.
details:
Project Overview and Purpose

ASTRA is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform developed for long-duration space missions. As astronauts travel farther from Earth, communication delays and temporary blackouts can make immediate medical assistance difficult to access. A one-way communication delay between Earth and Mars can reach approximately 22 minutes, meaning astronauts may need to assess health concerns and take appropriate initial action without waiting for an immediate response from Mission Control.

ASTRA addresses this challenge by bringing astronaut health monitoring, spacecraft environmental monitoring, cognitive assessments and emergency guidance together in one interactive dashboard. Its purpose is to help astronauts recognise changes in their health, understand potential risks and access appropriate next-step guidance, even when communication with Earth is limited.

How ASTRA Works

The platform follows a six-stage operational cycle:

*Monitor → Detect → Alert → Inform → Guide → Record.*

Astronauts can enter and track physiological measurements through the Data Input Hub, including heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, sleep duration, mood scores, reaction time, muscle strength and bone mineral density. Environmental readings, including cabin pressure, carbon dioxide partial pressure, inspired oxygen partial pressure, cabin temperature and radiation exposure, are displayed separately in the top section. The prototype uses configurable thresholds and individual pre-flight baselines to evaluate readings and identify unusual changes.

When a measurement falls outside its configured range, ASTRA assigns an appropriate status: GREEN for nominal conditions, YELLOW for caution and RED for critical conditions. It then displays visual and audible alerts, identifies the affected body system where relevant and provides structured, step-by-step guidance. Each reading and alert is recorded locally, allowing astronauts to review previous measurements and monitor changes over time.

Main Features and Functional Components

1. Interactive Human Body Explorer

ASTRA includes an interactive, vector-based 2D human body map with five clickable regions: the brain, heart, lungs, muscles and bones. Selecting a region opens its corresponding health panel, displaying relevant measurements, comparisons with personal baselines and historical graphs. For example, the brain panel includes sleep, cognitive performance, reaction time and mood tracking, while the cardiovascular panel displays heart rate and blood pressure. This anatomical approach makes health information easier to navigate and helps astronauts understand which body systems are being monitored.

2. Health Analytics and Personalised Monitoring

The dashboard uses interactive graphs to display health measurements and their changes over time. It includes reference ranges, personal baseline indicators and visual markers for caution and critical thresholds. Rather than relying only on a single reading, ASTRA allows astronauts to identify patterns and notice persistent changes that may require attention. Historical records can also be reviewed through tables and recent alert logs.

3. Cognitive and Behavioural Health Assessment

Long-duration missions can place considerable demands on attention, memory, sleep and mental wellbeing. ASTRA therefore includes two short cognitive exercises. The approximately 10-second reaction-time test measures response latency in milliseconds, while the memory and attention exercise evaluates visual pattern and sequence recall. Results are recorded and compared with individual performance baselines to help identify changes over time. The platform also tracks sleep duration and PHQ-4 mood screening scores. These features support monitoring and are not intended to diagnose psychological or neurological conditions.

4. Emergency Clinical Decision-Support Guidance

ASTRA includes nine structured guidance cards covering different environmental and biomedical hazards. These provide organised, numbered steps to help astronauts verify abnormal readings, recognise warning signs, follow appropriate monitoring procedures and understand when to escalate a concern to crew medical support or Mission Control. The guidance is designed to support decision-making using pre-approved procedures rather than replace medical professionals or independently prescribe treatment.

5. Daily Mission and Countermeasure Routine Tracker

The routine tracker organises daily activities into three sections: Morning Protocol, In-Flight Maintenance and Evening Review. These include health-record updates, hydration targets, exercise tracking, dosimeter checks, sleep monitoring and cognitive assessments. The In-Flight Maintenance section includes an ARED resistance-exercise checklist to support muscle and bone health in microgravity. Tasks are timestamped and retained so that astronauts can review their daily adherence and previous activity.

6. Environmental Monitoring and Alert System

ASTRA also considers the spacecraft environment, recognising that astronaut health is closely connected to cabin conditions. Its environmental monitoring interface tracks key indicators such as radiation exposure, cabin pressure, carbon dioxide, inspired oxygen and temperature. These readings are evaluated against configurable reference limits and mission-specific thresholds. Abnormal environmental conditions can trigger alerts and direct astronauts towards the relevant approved response checklist.

Technical Architecture and Tools Used

ASTRA was developed as a web-based application using HTML5, Tailwind CSS, custom CSS3 and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+). HTML5 provides the interface structure, while CSS and Tailwind CSS are used to create a consistent aerospace inspired design with clear visual indicators and accessible navigation.

JavaScript powers the platform's core logic, including data validation, threshold evaluation, baseline comparisons, alert management and interactions between dashboard components. The decision engine evaluates critical thresholds before caution thresholds so that the most serious applicable status is displayed. Chart.js is used to create interactive health graphs, while inline SVG provides the clickable anatomical body map. The Web Audio API generates distinct audio alerts for caution and critical conditions.

To support operation without an internet connection, ASTRA uses IndexedDB for local data persistence and a Progressive Web App architecture with a Service Worker for offline caching. New readings can be stored locally and marked as awaiting synchronisation until connectivity returns. The current prototype demonstrates this offline storage and synchronisation workflow locally, without depending on a live ground server.

The project also includes automated testing functions for its decision engine, alert behaviour and input validation. Its development documentation records more than 100 engine checks, 34 alert checks and additional data-validation cases, helping the team test how the application responds to normal, abnormal, missing and outdated readings.

Creativity and Innovation

ASTRA's main innovation is its integration of several astronaut health-support functions into one platform rather than treating them as separate tools. Its interactive anatomical explorer connects health measurements to the body systems they relate to, while its personalised graphs help users understand changes rather than simply view isolated numbers. The combination of environmental monitoring, cognitive assessments, colour-coded alerts, structured guidance and offline record keeping creates a more complete approach to astronaut self-monitoring.

The platform also uses a consistent decision-support cycle: it does not simply identify an abnormal measurement but connects that measurement to an alert, relevant information, recommended next steps and a recorded event. Its offline-first design is particularly important for exploration missions where communication with Earth may be delayed or temporarily unavailable.

Factors Considered During Development

Several operational and human factors shaped ASTRA's design:

- Communication delays: Astronauts may not receive immediate guidance from Earth, so essential monitoring information and guidance should remain accessible locally.

- Microgravity health risks: Changes in muscle strength, bone density, cardiovascular function and physical conditioning need to be monitored during extended missions.

- Radiation exposure: Cumulative exposure must be tracked against applicable mission-specific limits.

- Isolation and confinement: Sleep, mood, memory and cognitive performance are important aspects of crew wellbeing.

- Spacecraft environmental conditions: Cabin pressure, oxygen, carbon dioxide and temperature can affect crew safety and must be monitored alongside individual health.

- Individual differences: Astronauts have different pre-flight health measurements, making personal baselines important when evaluating changes.

- Ease of use under pressure: Clear graphs, accessible navigation, colour-coded warnings and numbered instructions help make information easier to understand.

- Data availability and reliability: Local storage and offline caching help preserve access to records and core application features during communication interruptions.

- Medical responsibility: ASTRA provides monitoring and decision support, not independent diagnosis or treatment. Serious concerns must be escalated through approved medical and mission procedures.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA aims to improve astronaut health awareness, support earlier recognition of potentially concerning changes and make relevant health information easier to access during long-duration missions. By combining physiological monitoring, environmental indicators, cognitive assessments and structured guidance, it gives crew members a central place to review their wellbeing and understand when further assistance may be required.

Its offline-first approach is intended to reduce dependence on continuous communication with Earth, while its historical records and personal baseline comparisons support more informed monitoring throughout a mission. The platform could also be adapted for future exploration habitats and other isolated environments where access to immediate medical support is limited.

Ultimately, ASTRA is designed to bring health information and decision support closer to the astronaut. It does not aim to replace doctors or Mission Control; instead, it helps astronauts better understand their health, recognise potential risks and take informed next steps when Earth is out of reach.
